sweep_summary: Polabian (pola1255) is in the catalog as weight-hedged (stress on the last non-reduced syllable: final if its vowel is full, else penult), deciding source Polański 2010, Gramatyka języka połabskiego, sec. 2.2.1 pp. 36-48 (rule p. 48). The search of works with stress or accent in the title turned up a single bibliography item, Eisenberg 1991 'Syllabische Struktur und Wortakzent. Prinzipien der Prosodik deutscher Wörter' (Zeitschrift für Sprachwissenschaft 10(1): 37-64): it is about German word stress, and Glottolog's link to Polabian is a machine keyword assignment (record 411095 language code field: 'Polabian [pox] (computerized assignment from "wortakzent")', page saved). Relevance another language or variety, priority none; the De Gruyter landing page and PDF link could not be reached by automated download/empty to our fetchers (Crossref lists CC BY-NC-ND, so it may open in a browser), not pursued since it says nothing about Polabian; it should be dropped from the pola1255 bibliography. No new Polabian stress source was found; the best first-hand statement read in this search of works with stress in the title is Kortlandt's open 'Polabian accentuation' (already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 check pass), p. 1: 'The stress fell on the last full vowel of a word form, which was found either in the final or in the penultimate syllable. In the latter instance, the final syllable contained a reduced vowel', which confirms the catalog's classification and does not supersede Polański 2010.

new_statements.quote: From a synchronic point of view, the accentuation of Late Polabian has been clarified by Trubetzkoy (1929) and Olesch (1973, 1974). The stress fell on the last full vowel of a word form, which was found either in the final or in the penulti-mate syllable. In the latter instance, the final syllable contained a reduced vowel. This rule was challenged by Kuryłowicz (1955), who maintained that the stress was fixed on the initial syllable of the word. [...] I therefore think that it is correct for an earlier stage of the language, which may conveniently be called Middle Polabian.

new_statements.reading: Late Polabian stress is right-edge and conditioned by vowel quality: it falls on the final syllable when that syllable's vowel is full, otherwise on the penult (the final then having a reduced vowel), i.e. on the last full (non-reduced) vowel of the word form. Kuryłowicz's fixed: initial syllable stress is accepted only for an earlier 'Middle Polabian' stage. This is the same rule as the catalog's deciding source, Polański 2010 p. 48 ('miejscem akcentu połabskiego była ostatnia niezredukowana sylaba wyrazu' = the place of Polabian stress was the last non-reduced syllable of the word; re-verified in the extracted text we hold at, folio 'GP.indb 47'/p. 48), and it confirms the weight-hedged coding (weight = full vs reduced vowel). Note: this file was already downloaded and logged as 'confirms' by the 2026-09-16 check pass ( fetched_now); it was re-read, not newly acquired, in this search of works with stress in the title.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's weight-sensitive (tentative) coding from Polański 2010 p. 48 ('miejscem akcentu połabskiego była ostatnia niezredukowana sylaba wyrazu' = last non-reduced syllable): final if its vowel is full, else penult; weight class full-vs-reduced vowel; right window. Kortlandt uses the same 'full vowel' vs 'reduced vowel' terms, not long vs short, so he also sides with Polański against reading the rule as vowel-length weight. He adds a diachronic layering (initial stress only for Middle Polabian) that the catalog does not need synchronically. The existing_statements entry for this same file already records this; nothing new.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Late (attested) Polabian: stress falls on the last syllable with a full (non-reduced) vowel; that is the final syllable when its vowel is full, otherwise the penult, in which case the final syllable has a reduced vowel. Right-edge, two-syllable window, 'weight' = full vs reduced vowel. Kuryłowicz's fixed initial stress is accepted by Kortlandt only for an earlier, unattested 'Middle Polabian' stage; pre-Polabian had Proto-Slavic mobile stress. The article's body is a diachronic account of how vowel reduction and the stress shifts produced this surface pattern (retraction from short final vowels, initial fixation, reduction after long vowels, then fixation on the last full vowel).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Late Polabian. Notes that most trisyllabic and all longer word forms have a reduced final vowel (so penult stress generalized there), and that trisyllabic forms with a stressed short medial vowel show no reduction (e.g. *želězo /zil'ozü/); loans are not discussed here (they are in Polański).
new_statements.identity_note: Kortlandt's rule is for 'Late Polabian', i.e. the attested Drawehn (Lüchow-Dannenberg) Polabian of the c. 1700 records; the same variety the catalog codes. His 'Middle Polabian' (initial stress) and 'pre-Polabian' (Proto-Slavic mobile stress) are reconstructed earlier stages, not attested varieties.

audit.reasoning: The classification (weight-hedged, right edge, weight = full vs reduced vowel: stress on the final syllable if its vowel is full, else the penult) rests on the standard modern reference grammar of Polabian by the field's leading specialist, held locally as the library's open PDF, and every quoted fragment was found verbatim at the cited pages (38, 40, 45, 47-48, rule on p.48). Polabian is extinct since the 18th century, so no instrumental study can supersede a philological reconstruction; Polański 2010 is the latest and fullest such reconstruction and reviews all rivals.
